body_en: A new student comes to our class today. She does not know any name here, and she does not know the way to the office. She looks at all the other students and feels very small. Then one student asks her a question about her old school. They begin to talk. After some minutes they laugh together. The new student says that she likes to read long stories. The other student says the same thing. Now they know that they can be friends. At the end of the day they leave the school together and walk into the town. The new student thinks that this day was good.

My mother gives me a very old book. She says that her own mother read this book many years ago. I take the book to my room and open it. In the book I find a letter. The letter is from a friend of my mother. In it the friend writes about a long train visit to another city. She writes about the food, the people and the water in that town. I read every word. Then I show the letter to my mother. She looks at it for a long time and does not say anything. Then she says that this friend was the best friend of her life. Now I keep the letter in the same book.

title_en: The best thing about the job
body_en: My mother works in a small shop in our town. Some days are hard and some days are good. Today many people come to the shop. They buy food and other things. My mother has no time to sit down. At the end of the day she is very late, but she feels good. She tells me that one old man came to the shop this week. He could not find the price of a book. My mother helped him, and he said thank you many times. Then he came back with all his family and bought more books. My mother says that this is the best thing about her job: not the money, but the people. I want to work with her one day.

My friend started a new job at a small company last month. On the first day she came very early. She did not know where to sit, and she did not want to ask. For one hour she stood and said nothing. Then a member of the staff called her name. He said that the others wanted to meet her. She followed him into a large room. Several people were talking about a new product. They asked her what she thought. She was quite sure that her idea was too small, but she said it. The others liked it a lot. Now she understands that the first day is hard for every person, and that no one expects a new member to know the whole system.

Our town has a market in the center. It opens early and stays open until late. My mother and I go there when we have enough time. The cost of food is quite low, and most of the people who work there are local. Last week we met a woman who has had the same place in the market for several years. She said that big companies offer a lower price, but people still come to her. They come because they know her name and they like to talk to her. My mother says that this is the value of a local market. It is not just a place to buy things; it is a part of the life of the town. I understand her now, although I did not understand this when I was young.

Last month my friend had to send a report to the government office. The report included figures about the local market and the cost of public programs. He started early, but a problem with the system stopped him for several days. He could not receive the last records from another office. He decided to call and ask for help. The person who answered his call said that the whole system was down, and that he should try again the next week. My friend did not want to lose more time, so he decided to send the report without those figures and to include a note about the problem. In fact, no one at the government office even asked about it. He now understands that it is better to send most of a report early than to send the whole report too late.

Last term our school decided to change its policy about late students. The head of the school insisted that every student must come before the first class. Some parents were not able to bring their children so early, and they said so. At first the school ignored them. Then one parent arranged a meeting and persuaded the others to come. It was obvious that both sides wanted the same thing: a school where students learn well. After a long process, the school changed the policy. Now a student who comes late must stay for one hour at the end of the day. This is not what all the parents wanted, but most people think that it is better than the old policy.

My friend leads a small group at a service company. For years she believed that a good leader must answer every question at once. She never hesitated. Then a member of her group told her that this made the others stop talking. So she tried something new: after every question she paused before she spoke. At first the pause felt too long, and she had little confidence in it. But within one month the group began to speak more. People who had never offered ideas now offered several. She acknowledged that she had been the problem, although this was hard to say. Now she believes that a leader who pauses is more reliable than one who always has the answer.

Our class arranged a meeting about the development of a new study program. The school had a fund for it, but it was unclear whether the money could be used for books or only for the building. Some students insisted that new books should be the first thing. Others said that the room required work more than the books did, and that no one could study well in it. Both sides had a belief that they were right, and for a while no one would hesitate to say so. Then one of the parents suggested a process: every person would write down one thing, and the group would consider all of them together. In the end the plan included both sorts of work, and every student felt that the group had heard them.

My colleague had to assess a new product before the company could offer it to the public. The assessment was extensive, and the outcome was not obvious. Some components worked well; others declined in value after a period of use. She perceived a fundamental problem: the whole system required constant support, and the company had no adequate staff for that. The head of her office urged her to ignore this and to report that the product was reliable. She would not do it. She acknowledged the benefit of the product, but she also illustrated the harm that could follow. In the end the company decided to withdraw the product for one year. Not all of her colleagues praised what she did, but no one could dismiss her figures. She had done what the circumstances required.

When the city office imposed a new restriction on local companies, no one anticipated the outcome. The policy was comprehensive, and its priority was the security of the public. But the procedure required every small company to consult a second office before it could offer any product to the market. For a large company this was a low cost. For a small one it was a barrier. Within one year several local companies had to withdraw from the market. The city office did not neglect the criticism; it began a new assessment. The assumption of the policy had been that all companies had the same capability, and that assumption could not be sustained. The restriction remains, but the procedure now excludes the smallest companies. This is a compromise. It is not what the companies wanted, but it works.

Members of the same staff can perceive the same result in different ways. Last month our group came to the end of a long process. One colleague evaluated it as a genuine achievement: the outcome exceeded every expectation, and the whole group had been consistent. Another colleague dismissed this view. He said that we had neglected one crucial component, and that the complexity of the system would threaten us later. At first I thought that only one of them could be right. Now I think that both were. The achievement was real, and the harm was also real. A comprehensive assessment must include both perspectives, although this makes it much harder to justify any outcome at all. Since then I have tried to consult the person who is least sure before I report that something worked.
